title: Clear Roadblocks Yourself

short.lead: A new rule would make me test every "I can't" claim, install missing tools myself, and never hand you a blocker I could clear; you pick how strongly it is enforced.
short.hint: Tap a step to see it.
items: Check the claim before making it

Before I say a tool, engine or machine is missing, I check. I use which (finds a program), ls (lists a folder), uname and hostname (name the machine), or list_computer_folders (lists folders on your PC). Claiming from memory is what went wrong on your PC. The session said Unity was not installed and that it was the wrong PC, and neither was true.

items.alt: Flow from claim to probe to verdict
items.caption: The probe sits between the claim and the verdict.

items: Missing tool: install it, then carry on

In bypass permission mode (where I run without asking you first), I install anything missing (apt, pip, npm or a download) and then re-run the step. In other modes I still install, and the usual permission prompt asks you. Only a purchase, a licence or a login is yours to do.
Nothing from you, except a purchase, a licence or a login.
If a route fails, I try the next one: another tool, an attached machine, a script or a different host. I stop only when every route has been tried, and my report lists each attempt.

items.caption: A stop must list every route tried.

items: Your approval is recorded as a line in the decisions log.
Pick an option under Your choices, then send the approval line with Copy my reply.

changes: Gains two duties: install what is missing, and try another route.
The existing rule already says a "can't be done" claim needs a test. This extends it from claims to actions: a failed test is not the end, the next step is the fix.
Today: a claim needs a test. A Stop check (it runs when I finish a reply) flags "can't" when no tool ran. A separate rule says I must not hand my labour to you.
New: a short section, plus a detail file titled "Roadblocks are mine to clear", linked from both of those rules.
You stop being asked to install or switch machines.
Included only if you pick option B or C under "How firmly should this be enforced?"
Flags replies that say "I can't", "not installed", "not on your machine", or "you need to install" when no probe or install ran this turn.
Today: the evidence check catches "can't" claims with no tool run at all.
New: it also catches the same claims after an unrelated tool ran, and "you need to install" hand-offs.
It blocks a reply once and names the check I should have run.
choices: first
How firmly should this be enforced?
A
Rule text only: a new section and detail file, no hook change
Smallest; relies on me following it, and the session on your PC shows that is not enough.
B
Rule plus a Stop check that blocks roadblock claims with no probe (my suggestion)
Catches the exact failure, reuses the existing evidence check, and needs one new test case in verify.py.
C
B, plus a line at session start in bypass mode saying installs are pre-approved
Strongest; adds text to every bypass session and depends on the hook being told which permission mode is active.
B closes the gap the rule alone leaves, without adding to every session's context.
second
What counts as yours, not mine?
A
Licences, logins, purchases and destructive actions only (my suggestion)
Matches the existing destructive-action and users-hands rules.
B
Also any install over a set size
Safer, but it brings back the stalls you asked me to stop.
Everything else is labour, which the rules already say is not yours.

wrapup.summary: This proposal adds a rule so I probe before claiming a blocker, install missing tools, and try other routes before stopping.
wrapup.changing: rules/house-rules.md, a new rules/detail/roadblocks.md, and in B or C the Stop check plus one verify.py case.
wrapup.blocking: Your pick of A, B or C on how firmly to enforce this, and your pick of A or B on what counts as yours.
wrapup.next: After you approve, I turn this into a build plan.
